title: Joe's late years: genius, band management and the bus
summary: Joe wrote tunes at night, was hard to understand because he did not drink, managed his own band and lost money. He bought a bus in Nashville and a mail truck and died young.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: No, I don't think he had any trouble with it. I don't know. Because he never complained. Never. He seemed to be well then. He seemed to be well all the time. But after he began to get older, he was always depressed. He was always thinking, thinking, thinking all the time. Sometimes at night, he'd jump up out of the bed. And I'd ask him, what on earth happened to jump up out of the bed? He said, something came to me, music. And he'd get up and get that carnet. And he'd blow them notes, whatever they were. And the next morning he'd put them together. Well, I didn't understand what it was all about. Did he write them down then? Yes, he would write them down. He'd write them down before he'd go back to bed and go to sleep. But as I said, I think Joe could have lasted longer. Had he been a fella, the fella would stick to understand. He was very hard to understand. Once you met him, you'd like it. But he was hard to understand. When a man don't drink with everybody, they don't understand you. Especially those kind of men. They expect you to drink with them. Then you'd talk a little bit more than you would talk if you didn't drink. And he didn't drink. He was hard. I had so many of his friends that tell me that they can't understand him. But he was really a genius. Yes, he must have been. He was really a genius. But as I said, he didn't want anybody to go ahead of a band, like to sell your band. He wanted to do all that himself. And he had no regular income. You know, if you take a band out on the road, or they sell your band, you've got to have money. He went to most every big place. He was losing money all the time. Because sometimes the fellas, he would get a big job after he got on the road. He'd get a big job. And they would demand the band to be at 7 o'clock. If it rained, if it doesn't rain before 7. If it rained, then the contract was broken. Now, some of the men was out gallivanting, drinking. He didn't know where to find them. He told me a lot of time he had to pick and pick the instrument out of pawn and all of that. He went through all of that. Well, it was hard on him. It was hard. And his last years was...
It must have been very bad, huh? Very bad. I heard he had a bus too and had trouble with that bus and all too.

He bought a bus in Nashville, Tennessee. And once he bought a... What do you call this? Truck? Truck actually. Mail truck. Oh, yeah. Mail truck. But that was to carry the band, the music and the instrument and all the music. And they wouldn't let him use that out there in Nashville, Tennessee. Well, they wouldn't let him use the mail truck. No, no. They wouldn't let him use that. He bought that to travel around. Yes. Go to little short places, you know. But, as I said, he was a happy-go-lucky sort of a fellow, in a way. He was like of a dial disposition because... And he'd do anything for you. Anything. Nothing was too much trouble. And his money wasn't too good to spend. But, I don't know, for some reason, I always say that the fellows didn't stick enough with Joe. I don't know why, but they were... Maybe he would have been living now, had he gone to somebody and tell him. And they could have given him an understanding how to do and how to get along. But he didn't. He kept it all to himself. And the last days, he wasn't so sick. He wasn't so sick. For a grand man. And like I said, just... If he'd have just lived five more years, he wouldn't realize what he was.
